questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a map description selects and omits.
questions.stem: Sheet 12 of the projected atlas records three features of the northern inlet and names no settlement on its shore.

options.text: The omission shows the sheet's purpose, since a navigation chart records navigable features and not people.
The omission shows poor practice, because every feature belongs on a chart at the same level.
options.misconception: believes completeness is the only measure of chart quality

options.text: The omission shows political pressure, because the cartographer was told.
options.misconception: invents an instruction the record does not mention

options.text: The omission shows careless work, because naming settlements is the quickest way to orient one on a coast.
options.misconception: assumes more features always make a better description

questions.explanation: A description is defined by what it selects for its purpose, and a navigation chart selects navigable features and drops the settlements. Poor practice, political pressure.
questions.hint: Ask what this particular sheet exists to do.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a comparison reveals that a single description cannot.
questions.stem: Projection 21 places the estuary settlement beside the hill village to show how differently each answered the same flood.

answer.exemplar: Setting the two settlements side by side lets the reader see that identical conditions produced opposite responses, so the comparison itself carries the argument rather than simply arranging information. The hill village raised its ground and the estuary village rebuilt on the same level, and placing them in one frame lets the difference in outcome emerge without a sentence of judgement.

questions.explanation: Comparison generates meaning that neither description alone could supply, since the reader measures one settlement against the other. Placing two places in one frame makes the divergence.
questions.hint: Ask what readers can see only by looking at both.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Analyse how a comparison of two places shapes the reader's judgement.
questions.stem: The projection for the western valley sets the terraced fields against the newly planted orchard and asks the reader to compare.

options.text: The comparison favours the terraces, since the reader sees them as tested and the orchard as untested ground.
options.misconception: reverses which side the comparison favours

options.text: The comparison favours the orchard, because readers see the terraces as worn beside something still unproven.
The comparison is neutral, because placing two land uses side by side asserts nothing about either of them.
options.misconception: believes juxtaposition makes no evaluative claim

options.text: The comparison is neutral, because a projection describes what exists and may not express preference.
options.misconception: treats description as free of evaluative effect

questions.explanation: Juxtaposition is evaluative even when no verdict is stated, because the attributes given to each side colour readers' view of both. Reversal, neutrality.
questions.hint: Ask which side gains by the qualities given to it.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Identify how a map legend's register differs from a travel book's.

stimulus.body: The legend for the provincial sheet uses a bare noun for each symbol class, without articles, verbs, or adjectives. The travel guide covering the same province, in the same project, describes the same features in continuous prose addressed to a reader who intends to go there. The editor asked whether the two should share a vocabulary.

questions.stem: Projection note 26 asks whether the legend and the guide should share a vocabulary.

options.text: They should, because shared vocabulary would make the two documents easier to use side by side.
options.misconception: prioritises convenience over the register each form needs

options.text: They should not, because the guide's register is too literary for a factual publication of any kind.
options.misconception: condemns narrative prose in factual work generally

options.text: They should not, because a legend's clipped register and the guide's narrative register do different jobs.
They should, because a project that produces one map should publish only one way of speaking about places.
options.misconception: assumes a single house voice across incompatible forms

questions.explanation: Register is chosen for the work the form performs, and a legend names classes for scanning while a guide narrates for one with intentions. Convenience, general literary prohibition.
questions.hint: Ask what each form makes the reader do.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate which details a description chooses as proof of its claim.
questions.stem: Projection 33 uses the depth of the harbour channel and the width of the lock as proof the port holds deep-draught traffic.

options.text: The selection is apt, since a reader who sees two precise figures assumes the claim is verified.
options.misconception: treats precision of figures as proof of the claim

options.text: The selection is weak, because depth and width say nothing about the silt that repeatedly fills the channel.
options.misconception: misses the silting that limits the claimed capacity

options.text: The selection is weak, since a description should never use measured figures when a painter's view is better.
options.misconception: rejects measurement on stylistic grounds alone

options.text: The selection is apt, since the two measurements decide whether a large vessel can be accommodated.

questions.explanation: Evidence is apt when it bears directly on the claim, and channel depth plus lock width are the measurements that determine whether deep-draught vessels fit. Precision, silting.
questions.hint: Ask what determines whether a large vessel fits.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Identify where a description places its emphasis and what that costs.
questions.stem: The projection for the border district spends a full column on the old boundary posts and one line on the farms.

options.text: Emphasis falls on the boundary posts, so the projection treats a legal trace as more important than the farms.
Emphasis falls on the farms, so the projection treats the daily economy as more significant than the boundary.
options.misconception: reverses where the emphasis falls

options.text: Emphasis is absent, because a projection that gives space to both subjects equally offers no preference.
options.misconception: mistakes unequal space for an absence of emphasis

options.text: Emphasis falls on the boundary posts, since the sheet's subject is the boundary and farms are context.
options.misconception: reads the emphasis as a statement of official scope

questions.explanation: Space is emphasis, and a full column against a single line shows the projection placing the boundary posts above the farms in significance. Reversal, equal treatment.
questions.hint: Ask which subject received the greater space.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain the connotative difference between two words for the same feature.
questions.stem: Projection 38 records why the draft called the wetland a marsh and the final sheet calls it fen.

answer.exemplar: Marsh and fen are not synonyms, and the swap changes what a reader expects. Marsh carries the sense of something unstable and half formed, which would suggest a place worth draining, while fen suggests ground that is wet by nature and holds what it holds, so the final wording resists the implication of the earlier one and the whole argument about drainage shifts with the term.

questions.explanation: Diction carries connotations beyond the referent, and marsh suggests improvable ground while fen suggests ground that is wet by nature. The single substitution changes readers' expectation.
questions.hint: Ask what each word implies can be done to the land.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the effect of describing a place through one dominant sense.
questions.stem: Sheet 44 of the coastal projection describes the harbour entirely in sound, and the cartographer's note defends that choice.

options.text: The choice makes the place particular, because a sound only description is the most accurate kind.
options.misconception: confuses particularity with factual accuracy

options.text: The choice makes the place particular, since a reader who hears the harbour hears that harbour alone.
The choice weakens the place, since a description that omits sight and size gives the reader no sense of it.
options.misconception: assumes description must cover every sense

options.text: The choice weakens the place, because a projection records measurable features and sounds are not measurable.
options.misconception: restricts description to measurable features

questions.explanation: A description restricted to one sense becomes particular rather than thin, since the reader receives the distinctive qualities of that place. Accuracy, comprehensiveness.
questions.hint: Ask what one gets instead of an inventory of features.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Analyse a comparison drawn between two unlike kinds of thing.

stimulus.body: The projection compares the spread of the market town to the spread of the network of footpaths radiating from it, and the caption asks whether the two shapes match. The survey was drawn from a surveyor's notebook in which the comparison was first tried as a question to himself.

questions.stem: Projection 49 asks whether the shape of the town matches the shape of the paths.

options.text: The comparison fails, because towns and footpaths are different kinds of thing and cannot be compared.
options.misconception: denies that unlike things may be compared

options.text: The comparison holds, because the surveyor's notebook says the paths came first and the town grew after.
options.misconception: grounds the finding in an external document not the shapes

options.text: The comparison holds, because the two shapes correspond point.
The comparison fails, since a projection records the present and cannot support claims about growth over time.
options.misconception: denies that a present record can imply history

questions.explanation: Comparing unlike things can produce a real finding when they share a formal property, and a town matching the shape of its paths shows that. Incomparability denies the yield.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two shapes correspond.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Synthesise how two descriptions of the same place can be read against each other.
questions.stem: Projection 54 compares the official sheet's description of the village with the resident's own account in the project archive.

options.text: They can be read against each other, since the official sheet is wrong wherever the accounts differ.
options.misconception: treats disagreement as error on one side only

options.text: They cannot be read against each other, because only the official sheet belongs in a publication of this kind.
options.misconception: denies the resident's account standing as evidence

options.text: They cannot be read against each other, because a comparison of two accounts of one place yields only opinion.
options.misconception: believes comparison can never yield knowledge

options.text: They can be read against each other, because each describes the same ground with different priorities.

questions.explanation: Two accounts of the same ground can be set beside each other since their differing priorities reveal what each side counts as present. One side's error, excluded testimony.
questions.hint: Ask what the gaps between the two accounts disclose.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the register used to address a reader in a hazard warning.
questions.stem: The avalanche sheet for the northern slope uses clipped commands where the guide beside it uses long explanatory sentences.

options.text: The sheet's imperative register suits a hazard.
The sheet's imperative register is unsuitable.
options.misconception: believes formal documents must avoid the imperative

options.text: The sheet's imperative register is unsuitable, because the guide's explanatory sentences are more reliable.
options.misconception: confuses sentence length with reliability

options.text: The sheet's imperative register suits a hazard, because commands are shorter and shorter is better in a hurry.
options.misconception: reduces register choice to brevity alone

questions.explanation: Register is chosen for readers' situation, and a person in a hazard needs the instruction rather than the explanation. Rules about formality, brevity as virtue.
questions.hint: Ask what readers need in the moment.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the choice of evidence reflects the claim being made.
questions.stem: Projection 58 asks why the argument for the new rail link is supported by timetables but not by the towns it would connect.

answer.exemplar: The evidence offered is all about movement, since the claim being made is that the existing network moves people badly. Timetables establish delay and irregularity directly, so they support the claim exactly, while the towns the line would serve are drawn from a different argument about benefit that the sheet does not attempt. Selecting evidence is never neutral: it defines the size of the claim that can be made.

questions.explanation: Evidence is chosen to fit the claim, and timetables speak to delay and irregularity without needing anything about the towns. The unmentioned towns mark the boundary.
questions.hint: Ask what the evidence talks about and what the claim needs.

questions.learningObjective: Analyse how the placement of emphasis shapes a reader's priorities.
questions.stem: The projection for the mining valley prints the yield figures in bold and the casualty figures in a footnote.

options.text: The typography sets the yield as readers' priority, because bold type marks the most important figure.
options.misconception: explains the effect by typographic convention only

options.text: The typography sets the yield as readers' priority.
The typography sets the casualties as readers' priority.
options.misconception: assumes placement signals importance rather than suppression

options.text: The typography sets no priority, because readers consult the tables by row and ignore type weight.
options.misconception: assumes readers ignore visual hierarchy

questions.explanation: Typography directs attention, and bold yield figures against footnoted casualties make output the primary concern while human cost becomes marginal. Convention, hidden importance.
questions.hint: Ask which figure the eye reaches first.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain the connotative work done by a neutral-sounding word.

stimulus.body: The draft caption described the terraced hillside as an orderly arrangement of plots. A reviewer's comment asked whether the word orderly was doing more work than a caption should allow. The cartographer's reply is recorded in the file.

questions.stem: Projection 62 asks whether the word orderly in the caption carries too much.

options.text: It does not, because orderly is a neutral term for a regular pattern and the terraces are regular.
options.misconception: confuses accurate description with neutral implication

options.text: It does not, because captions are expected.
options.misconception: grants captions unlimited licence to praise

options.text: It does, because orderly praises the arrangement and quietly absolves whoever cut the terraces.
It does, because the terraces were laid out by surveyors, so the word rightly credits them.
options.misconception: redirects the objection to a question of historical credit

questions.explanation: A descriptive word can carry an implicit verdict, and orderly launders the history of cutting terraces into natural-looking regularity. Neutrality, generous licence.
questions.hint: Ask what the word praises and whom it excuses.

questions.learningObjective: Choose the description that best fits a stated purpose.
questions.stem: Projection 67 asks which of three candidate captions best serves the touring map's purpose.

options.text: The third, because it contains the most measurements, which makes the caption the most useful of the three.
options.misconception: substitutes quantity of figures for fitness of purpose

options.text: The first, because it gives the fullest history of the site, and history always belongs in a public caption.
options.misconception: assumes historical detail is always wanted by a walker

options.text: The first, because it is the longest, and length signals the care taken with the place.
options.misconception: treats length as evidence of care

options.text: The third, because it names what a walker can see from the path.

questions.explanation: A caption should be measured against the purpose of the map that carries it, and the walker's view at a glance is what the touring map exists to deliver. Measurement, historical fullness.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a comparison gains by being made between a place and a process.
questions.stem: The projection for the quarry district likens the face of the quarry to a wound that has begun to close over.

options.text: The likening argues that the damage is permanent.
The likening argues that the damage is permanent, because a wound closing over shows healing underway.
options.misconception: reverses what a closing wound signifies

options.text: The likening is decorative, because figurative comparison has no place in a projection meant for engineers.
options.misconception: excludes figurative language from technical work

options.text: The likening is decorative, because the quarry face is described in the survey with exact measurements.
options.misconception: assumes precise measurement removes the need for emphasis

questions.explanation: A metaphor can carry an argument, and a wound that closes over but never returns to whole argues for permanence. Underway healing, decoration, and redundant measurement each misread the likening.
questions.hint: Ask what a closing wound still shows about the surface.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Analyse what a comparative reading across two eras reveals.
questions.stem: Projection 71 asks what becomes visible when the projection overlays the shoreline of 1890 against the shoreline of today.

answer.exemplar: The overlay makes the loss legible in a way neither shoreline can be alone, because the reader sees the older line sitting inland of the new one and the difference becomes an area rather than a fact. Each single survey records a coastline accurately; placed together they record a rate of retreat and, with it, the argument that the coast here is not a fixed boundary but something in motion.

questions.explanation: Comparison reveals change that a single record cannot show, because the difference between two shorelines becomes a visible area. Accuracy of each survey and the coast as a fixed boundary each fail.
questions.hint: Ask what the area between the two lines means.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish two registers used for the same instruction.

stimulus.body: The fire evacuation card for the depot prints a sequence of plain commands in the imperative. The safety officer noted that both documents are approved and both are in use.

questions.stem: Projection 75 asks why the same procedure is printed in two different registers.

options.text: Because the card serves a moment of panic and the training version serves preparation.
options.misconception: reduces the choice to brevity rather than situation

options.text: Because the card serves a moment of panic and the training version serves a moment of preparation.
Because one of the two documents is out of date and should be withdrawn from circulation soon.
options.misconception: assumes a difference of register signals an error

options.text: Because the two registers are interchangeable.
options.misconception: assumes register makes no difference to comprehension

questions.explanation: The same procedure needs different registers for different hours, and commands suit panic while negotiated language suits preparation. Brevity, an outdated document.
questions.hint: Ask when each document will be read.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Judge whether a piece of evidence is strong enough for the claim made.
questions.stem: Projection 79 considers a projection that claims the valley's roads have improved and supports the claim with a single photograph.

options.text: The evidence is too weak, because photographs are unreliable and only measurements can support any claim.
options.misconception: dismisses visual evidence entirely

options.text: The evidence is strong, because a photograph persuades a general reader more effectively than a table.
options.misconception: judges evidence by persuasive force rather than adequacy

options.text: The evidence is too weak, because one photograph shows one moment.
The evidence is strong, because the photograph was taken at the worst point of the season and shows the roads.
options.misconception: invents a seasonal claim the record does not make

questions.explanation: Evidence must be adequate for the claim, and a single photograph of one road at one moment cannot establish a valley-wide trend. Dismissing photographs, persuasive force.

options.misconception: reads final position as intellectual openness

options.text: It weakens the argument, because a caption that names its own weaknesses invites the reader.
options.misconception: misses that the ending still lands a verdict

options.text: It changes nothing, because emphasis in a caption is a question.
options.misconception: reduces emphasis to typography only

options.text: It strengthens the argument, because placing the completed defences.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a technical term carries a value judgement in a popular projection.
questions.stem: The public projection for the fishery uses the word harvest in its caption where the technical sheets use extraction.

options.text: Harvest carries a pleasant connotation, so the word softens the activity and nudges readers to accept it.
Harvest carries a pleasant connotation, so the word softens the activity and warns the reader.
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the connotative effect

options.text: Harvest is strictly a more technical term than extraction, so the change makes the caption more accurate.
options.misconception: treats the change as an increase in technicality

options.misconception: reduces the substitution to a loss of precision

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a description's order shapes the reader's impression.
questions.stem: Projection 86 asks why the settlement description lists the smell of the place before anything visible.

answer.exemplar: The smell comes first, and that order sets the terms on which everything after it is read. A reader who has been given the smell of the tannery before seeing the yard will find the yards, the roofs and the river differently, because the smell has already told the reader what kind of place this is and what work happens there. Description is not a neutral inventory; the sequence is one of its arguments.

questions.explanation: Order in a description conditions the reading of what follows, and a smell placed first interprets every later detail. A neutral inventory and an afterthought framing each miss sequence's work.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader knows when the visual details arrive.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a comparison identifies what is distinctive in a place.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a register shift signals a change of audience within a document.
questions.stem: Projection 93 explains why the technical appendix of the survey changes its voice partway through.

answer.exemplar: The appendix begins in the impersonal register of a measurement record and then, where it discusses what the measurements mean for drainage, shifts to a plainer voice that addresses the reader directly. questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Analyse how emphasis created by silence works in a projection.
questions.stem: The projection for the estuary records two years of silting in full detail and says nothing about the dredging in between.

answer.exemplar: The sheet gives the silting its full weight, with year by year figures and a map of the channel, and it gives the dredging nothing at all. That silence is a choice with a direction: because the reader is never told that the channel was repeatedly cleared, the silting reads as a natural process, and the reader will judge the engineers' inaction as the cause of the loss rather than the relentless tide they were in fact fighting.

questions.explanation: Silence in a description is a choice with a direction, and omitting the dredging lets a natural process appear where people were constantly intervening. Spared detail, neutrality.
questions.hint: Ask what readers are being allowed to believe happened.

options.misconception: treats brevity as the test of a caption word

options.text: The word adds nothing, because open ground carries no expectation that the projection would be contradicting.
options.misconception: assumes a caption's words make no promises

options.text: The word imports a promise of comfort, so it presents a strip.

questions.explanation: An abstract noun in a caption promises a state rather than recording a feature, and relief sells unoccupied ground as a remedy. Word economy and the neutrality.
questions.hint: Ask what the word promises the reader the land will do.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a description can be accurate and still mislead.
questions.stem: Projection 156 asks how a description of the flooded flats can be true in every particular and still mislead.

answer.exemplar: The flats are described as level, well drained and regularly flooded, and each of those statements is true of the land as it was mapped. What the description leaves out is the works that made it so: the embankments that kept the river out and the pumps that drained what was let in, and once those are removed from the sentence the reader is left with a picture of naturally recurring inundation that the engineers had spent a century preventing.

questions.explanation: A description can be factually true in every stated particular and still mislead by leaving the human works out of the frame. Omission of the making turns an engineered landscape into a natural one.
questions.hint: Ask what the description leaves out of the picture.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Synthesise how a comparison can carry an argument about the present.
questions.stem: Projection 159 asks how the comparison of the town's current boundaries with its old ones supports a claim about expansion.

options.text: It supports the claim, since the enclosed area has grown and the boundary reaches land once excluded.
It supports the claim, because the older boundary was drawn by the same method.
options.misconception: credits method rather than the growth the figures show

options.text: It undermines the claim, because a comparison with the past shows only that things change.
options.misconception: mistakes change in the abstract for a rebuttal of growth

options.text: It undermines the claim, because the old boundary was drawn.
options.misconception: invents a motive for the earlier survey

questions.explanation: Comparing a current boundary with an older one shows how much land the town holds, and that difference supports a claim about expansion. Method uniformity and a flattering old line each misread it.
questions.hint: Ask what the enclosed area does between the two surveys.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a comparison whose terms have drifted between the two documents compared.

stimulus.body: The projected comparison sets the parish of the old survey against the parish of the modern one, and the note records that the two parishes have never covered the same ground: the older unit included a hamlet later transferred to a neighbouring parish, and the modern unit includes ground that was never parish land at all. The editor asked whether the comparison should run at all.

questions.stem: Projection 162 asks whether the comparison between the two parishes should be published.

options.text: It should, provided the sheet states that the units differ.
options.misconception: treats every change as sufficient warrant for a comparison

options.text: It should, provided the sheet states that the units differ in extent.
It should not, because a comparison between unlike units produces a figure that cannot mean anything.
options.misconception: treats a drifting comparison as meaningless not qualified

options.text: It should not, since the drift in the parish boundary means the older survey measured the wrong thing.
options.misconception: dismisses the earlier measure as wholly mistaken

questions.explanation: A comparison between units that have drifted is still informative if the sheet declares the drift. The divergence is itself the finding, not a defect.
questions.hint: Ask what the difference.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Judge the register of a projected account and its effect on the reader's trust.
questions.stem: Projection 165 asks what a steadily conversational register does to the reader's trust in a technical projection.

options.text: It builds trust, because a conversational register is the one professional readers respond to most warmly.
options.misconception: grounds the effect in reader preference rather than candour

options.text: It weakens trust, because a friendly voice.
options.misconception: reads candour as salesmanship rather than the reverse

options.text: It builds trust, because a plain spoken manner suggests a writer with nothing.
It changes nothing, since readers judge technical projections by their figures alone and never by voice.
options.misconception: denies that voice has any effect on a reader

questions.explanation: A plain conversational manner in a technical document reads as candour, and the reader takes the voice as evidence that the figures have not been dressed up. Warmth, persuasion.
questions.hint: Ask what the manner suggests about the figures.
